title: Clarifications to the DNS Specification
summary: This standards-track document identifies problem areas in the specification of the Domain Name System and proposes remedies for the defects. It clarifies details about how records and servers behave.

eli5.summary: A note fixing spots in the phone book's instructions that people misread.

questions: rrset ttl and dns server behavior
what is an rrset in dns
what is the maximum dns ttl
can an ns record point to a cname
when is the dns tc bit set
subtitle: Fixes the spots in the original DNS specs that implementers kept reading differently.

tldr.problem: The original DNS specifications left several details unclear or widely ignored, such as which source address a multi-homed server replies from, whether records of one name and type may have different TTLs, and what counts as a valid name.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2181 states the intended behavior for eight separate issues: reply source address, RRSets, zone cuts, SOA records, the TTL, the TC bit, canonical names and name syntax.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1034, RFC 1035 and RFC 1123, and it has since been updated by several later RFCs.

facts.label: TTL encoding
facts.value: Low 31 bits of the 32-bit field; top bit zero

today: RFC 2181 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1034, RFC 1035 and RFC 1123. It has itself been updated by RFC 2535, RFC 4033, RFC 4034, RFC 4035, RFC 4343, RFC 5452 and RFC 8767.

sections.title: Scope of the Clarifications
sections.content:
RFC 2181 collects problem areas in the Domain Name System specification (RFC 1034 and RFC 1035) that had been noted over the years. The issues are independent of one another. The abstract lists eight: reply addresses from multi-homed servers, TTLs in sets of records with the same name, class and type, zone cuts, three minor SOA issues, the precise definition of the TTL, the TC (truncated) bit, what an authoritative or canonical name is, and what makes a valid DNS label.

The first six are areas where correct behavior was unclear. The last two were already adequately specified, but the specifications were sometimes ignored, so the memo reinforces them.

The memo deliberately avoids the words MUST, SHOULD and MAY. It says that wherever it states that something should or must be done, or that a behavior is acceptable or not, that is a fundamental part of the specification regardless of the wording. Only behavior that is truly optional is stated as optional.
sections.eli5: The note is a list of eight places where the old rulebook was unclear, plus a promise that every 'should' in it really means it.

sections.title: Where Replies Come From
sections.content:
DNS clients expect a reply to come from the same address the query was sent to. The address, together with the message identifier, is used to match replies to queries and to filter out spurious responses. Some multi-homed hosts running DNS servers answered from a different source address, so clients discarded the replies as unsolicited.

For UDP, a server must send the reply with the IP source address set to the destination address of the query packet. If that address is not permitted for this purpose, the reply may come from any legal address allocated to the server, chosen to maximize the chance that the client can use it for further queries. Servers need particular care with anycast, multicast or similar addresses.

Replies must be directed to the port the query came from, and should be sent from the port the query was directed to. Except in extraordinary circumstances, that is the well known DNS port.
sections.eli5: If you ask a question at the front door, the answer should come back from that same door. Otherwise you will think a stranger is talking to you and ignore it.

sections.title: Resource Record Sets
sections.content:
Each resource record (RR) has a label, class, type and data. Records with the same label, class and type but different data form a Resource Record Set (RRSet). Two records equal in all four parts are meaningless, and servers should suppress such duplicates.

A query returns the whole RRSet. If the set does not fit, the response must be marked as truncated. The TTLs of all RRs in an RRSet must be the same, and use of differing TTLs is deprecated, because it could produce partial replies from a caching server when only some of the TTLs have expired. A client that receives differing TTLs should treat this as an error: ignore the set if it came from a non-authoritative source, or, if the source is authoritative, act as if every TTL were the lowest one. A server may never send an RRSet with unequal TTLs.

Servers must never merge RRs from a response with cached RRs to form an RRSet. They either ignore the response or discard the cached set. An RRSet should also appear only once in a reply, except where a specification requires otherwise, as with the SOA record at the start and end of an AXFR response.

The memo also covers special cases for the DNSSEC record types SIG and NXT of that era. It warns that this information may become outdated as DNS Security matures.
sections.eli5: A set of records is like all the phone numbers listed under one person's name. You always get the whole list together, and every number on it has the same expiry date.

sections.title: Ranking Data by Trustworthiness
sections.content:
When a server must choose between a reply and what it already has cached, it should consider how trustworthy each source is. Authoritative answers replace data cached from additional information, but additional information is ignored if the cache holds data from an authoritative answer or a zone file.

The order from most to least trustworthy starts with data from a primary zone file (other than glue), then zone transfer data (other than glue), then the answer section of an authoritative reply, then the authority section of an authoritative answer, then glue. Data from the answer section of non-authoritative answers comes next. Additional information and the authority section of non-authoritative answers rank lowest.

The least trustworthy data should not be cached so that it could ever be returned as an answer, only as additional information. Otherwise its trustworthiness would be raised without cause. When DNSSEC is in use, authenticated and verified data is more trustworthy than unauthenticated data of the same type.
sections.eli5: If two people tell you different things, you believe the one who read it from the original book over the one who heard it secondhand.

sections.title: Zone Cuts and SOA Records
sections.content:
The DNS tree is divided into zones, separated by zone cuts. A cut is indicated in the parent zone by NS records naming the child zone's origin, and a child zone has no explicit reference to its parent. Every zone has an NS record at its origin and an SOA record as mandatory records. A server should not give authoritative answers for names in another zone, including the NS records at a cut, unless it also serves that other zone. Other than the DNSSEC cases, a server should ignore anything at a cut except NS records and the A records needed to find those servers.

Three SOA points are clarified. The SOA belongs in the authority section of an authoritative answer, not the additional section. The old line in RFC 1035 that an SOA TTL should always be sent as zero has not generally been implemented, and implementations should not assume it (nor are they required to send zero). The MNAME field should name the primary server for the zone, not the zone itself.
sections.eli5: A zone cut is the border between two neighboring countries. The border town's sign belongs to the country on the far side, and a guard from the other country should not claim to speak for it.

sections.title: TTL and the TC Bit
sections.content:
The TTL is defined as an unsigned number with a minimum of 0 and a maximum of 2147483647 (2^31 - 1). It is carried in the low 31 bits of the 32-bit TTL field, with the most significant bit set to zero. Implementations should treat a received TTL with that top bit set as zero. They may cap any TTL at an upper bound of their own, because the TTL is a maximum time to live, not a mandatory one.

The TC bit should be set only when an RRSet that is required for the response could not fit entirely. It should not be set just because extra information, such as additional section processing results, did not fit. In that case the whole RRSet that did not fit is omitted and TC stays clear. A client that sees TC set should ignore that response and ask again by a mechanism that allows larger replies, such as a TCP connection.
sections.eli5: A TTL is a 'use by' date on the answer. The TC bit is a flag saying 'this answer got cut off, ask again with a bigger envelope'.

sections.title: Canonical Names, CNAME and Name Syntax
sections.content:
Nothing in the DNS requires a host to have exactly one official name. A CNAME record provides the canonical name for an alias, and only one canonical name is allowed per alias. For any domain name, exactly one holds: one CNAME exists (optionally with SIG, NXT and KEY records), or one or more non-CNAME records exist, or the name exists with no records, or it does not exist. The memo calls the label of a CNAME record an alias, not 'a CNAME'.

A PTR record may have several RRs in its set, and its value must not be an alias. The domain name in an NS record, or in an MX record, must not be an alias either. Additional section processing does not follow CNAMEs, so an alias there would cost extra queries and can make some requests fail.

On syntax, the DNS limits only length: a label is 1 to 63 octets and a full name is 255 octets including separators. Any binary string may be a label, and implementations must not restrict labels. Applications may impose their own restrictions and must validate the data they use.
sections.eli5: A nickname can point to one real name, and the real name must be a real entry, not another nickname. Names can be almost anything, as long as they are not too long.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document states that it does not consider security. Section 4 is not related to security, and neither is the trust ordering in section 5.4.1. Security of DNS data is expected from Secure DNS (RFC 2065), which is mostly orthogonal to this memo.

It is not believed that anything here adds to existing DNS security issues. Correct implementation might help limit the spread of non-malicious bad data, but only DNSSEC can help against deliberate attempts to subvert DNS data.
sections.eli5: This note is about getting the rules clear, not about stopping bad guys. Stopping bad guys is a job for a different tool.
